chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Al-Numan, from Ubayd Allah ibn Musa, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim Al-Nakha'i, who said:

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Ali — they inherit the close relatives (dhawi al-arham) to the exclusion of the mawali (freedmen/patrons). I asked, 'And what about Ali (peace be upon him)?' He said, 'He was the most intense of the two.'

key_terms.أَشَدَّهُمَا: The more intense/strict of the two
key_terms.ذَوِي الْأَرْحَامِ: Close relatives (those with kinship ties but not fixed heirs)

ai.seo_question: Who inherits close relatives (dhawi al-arham) according to the view of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Ali?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the juristic preference for blood kinship (*dhawi al-arham*) over manumission ties (*mawali*) in inheritance, a view championed by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Ali. Notably, it elevates Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) as the most emphatic proponent of this hierarchy, reflecting the Shia emphasis on familial bonds superseding contractual or manumission relationships. This distinction underscores the theological and legal prioritization of lineage in Shia inheritance jurisprudence.
